 R/ggplot2 programming - Aesthetics must either be length one, or the same length as the dataProblems
    Riad KACED <riad....@gmail.com> Nov 18 12:44PM -0800  

    Dear follow R/ggplot users,
     
    I am fairly new to R/ggplot and I stumbling on an issue that I’m sure is
    easy to fix.
    I would like to make a plot with X values as a subset of the measurement
    and Y-values as another subset of the measured data.
     
    In the example as below, I have 4 products p1, p2,p3 and p4. Each are
    priced according to their skew, color and version.
    I would like to create a multi-facet plot that depicts the P3 prodcuts
    (Y-axis) vs P1 products (X-axis).
     
    My attempt as below has failed miserably with the following error:
    Error: Aesthetics must either be length one, or the same length as the
    dataProblems:subset(price, product == "p1"), subset(price, product == "p3")
     
    library(ggplot2)
    product=c("p1","p1","p1","p1","p1","p1","p1","p1","p2","p2","p2","p2","p2","p2","p2","p2","p3","p3","p3","p3","p3","p3","p3","p3","p4","p4","p4","p4","p4","p4","p4","p4")
    skew=c("b","b","b","b","a","a","a","a","b","b","b","b","a","a","a","a","b","b","b","b","a","a","a","a","b","b","b","b","a","a","a","a")

    color=c("C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2","C1","C2")
    price=c(3.39,3.6,3.76,4.02,2.44,2.57,2.78,2.96,3.18,3.38,3.64,3.88,2.15,2.26,2.54,2.7,3.1,3.06,3.52,3.58,2.13,2.07,2.5,2.53,2.98,2.83,3.55,3.49,1.81,1.71,2.24,2.22)
    df = data.frame(product, skew, version, color, price)
    # First plot all the data
    p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=price, y=price, colour=factor(skew))) +
    geom_point(size=2, shape=19)
    p1 <- p1 + facet_grid(version ~ color)
    p1 # This gavea very good plot. So far so good

    Riad.

    Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> Nov 18 02:06PM -0800  

    Hi:
     
    I think you need to reshape your data from long to wide to achieve
    what you want. This is my best guess as to what you're after; if this
    is totally off base you'll need to explain what you want more clearly.
     
    library(reshape2)
    library(ggplot2)
     
     
    # Reshape the data from long to wide:
    dfc <- dcast(df, skew + version + color ~ product, value.var = "price")
     
    # Plot
    ggplot(dfc, aes(x = p1, y = p3, color = factor(skew))) +
    geom_point() + facet_grid(color ~ version, labeller = label_both) +
    labs(x = "Product 1 price", y = "Product 3 price", color = "skew")
     
    It's often a good idea to use the labeller when you have two faceting
    variables; label_both prints both the factor name and level in a
    strip.
     
    Dennis
     

     

    Vivek Patil <pat...@gmail.com> Nov 18 02:11PM -0800  

    Or you may be after this:
     
    An alternative to Dennis' suggestion: Modify the last two lines to:
     
    p1 <- ggplot(subset(df, product=='p1'),aes(x=price))+
    geom_point(data=subset(df, product=='p3'),aes(y=price, color=skew))
    p1
     
    Following Ben's point of avoiding subset: use :
     
    p1 <- ggplot(df[df$product=='p1',],aes(x=price))+
    geom_point(data=df[df$product=='p3',],aes(y=price, color=skew))
    p1

 Create several plots and save as files
    Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> Nov 18 10:47AM -0800  

    Hi:
     
    One way to go about this is to write a function to get a single plot and to
    use one of the apply family functions to map it to each sub-data frame
    associated with unique exposure levels. The plyr package is useful in this
    regard.
     
    # Function to generate the plot
    plotfun <- function(d)
    {
    require(ggplot2)
    p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = lags)) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(y = est, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), size = 1)
    pname <- paste0(as.character(d$exposure[1]), ".pdf")
    ggsave(p, file = pname)
    invisible()
    }
     
    # Map it to each exposure group: the _ indicates that nothing should be
    # saved since a side effect is performed (i.e., saving the graphs)
    library(plyr)
    d_ply(df, .(exposure), plotfun)
     
    I got three saved plots from this code, as expected. The plot function is
    simple, so tailor it to your needs.
     
    Dennis
